readingInstruction: Read Jeremiah 46:1-48:47. This is a survey day. These are oracles against Egypt, the Philistines, and Moab. Do not worry about every name. Read for the repeated message: God is Lord of the nations, and pride is judged.
settingTheScene: Chapters 46 to 51 are Jeremiah’s oracles against the nations. Like Isaiah 13-23 and Ezekiel 25-32, they place the story of Judah inside God’s rule over the world. The first oracle is against Egypt, tied to the battle of Carchemish in 605 BC. The next ones concern the Philistines and Moab, with echoes of Isaiah’s earlier oracles on Moab. These oracles show that no nation escapes God’s judgment and that some of them receive a promise of restoration.
observation: “Who is this, rising like the Nile, like rivers whose waters surge?” (46:7).
“Egypt rises like the Nile… I will surely punish Amon of Thebes, and Pharaoh” (46:8, 25).
“But fear not, O Jacob my servant, nor be dismayed, O Israel” (46:27).
“I will make a full end of all the nations among whom I have scattered you, but of you I will not make a full end” (46:28).
“Because you trusted in your works and your treasures, you also shall be taken” (48:7).
“We have heard of the pride of Moab… his insolence, his pride, and his arrogance” (48:29).
“Cursed is he who does the work of the LORD with slackness” (48:10).
“Yet I will restore the fortunes of Moab in the latter days, declares the LORD” (48:47).
interpretation:
The oracle against Egypt begins with a military scene: the Egyptian army at Carchemish, preparing for battle, and then fleeing in defeat. “Who is this, rising like the Nile?” The question has the same shape as Isaiah’s against Babylon. Egypt rose in pride, as a flood that covers the earth, but the LORD is greater. The oracle ends in 46:27-28 with comfort for Israel: “Fear not, O Jacob my servant.” God will discipline in just measure, but will not destroy his people.

The oracle against the Philistines in chapter 47 pictures waters from the north that sweep over the land, and the cries of fathers who do not turn to help their children. It is a picture of utter terror.

Chapter 48 is a long lament over Moab, the nation descended from Lot and often hostile to Israel. The reason for its fall is stated clearly: it trusted in its works and treasures, and in its pride. “Moab has been at ease from his youth… like wine left on its dregs.” A people that has never been disturbed grows complacent. The prophet’s sorrow is real: “Therefore I wail for Moab; I cry out for all Moab.” This is no gloating.

Notice 48:10: “Cursed is he who does the work of the LORD with slackness.” It is a warning to the executioners of judgment, but also to everyone. The work of the LORD is serious.

The chapter ends with a surprise. “Yet I will restore the fortunes of Moab in the latter days.” Even this enemy nation has a future. The God who judges the nations is the God who will bring them back. Jeremiah’s prophecies of judgment are never the last word.
connection: Revelation 18 and 19 draw on the oracles against the nations for the fall of Babylon. Colossians 3:23 says, “Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord.” Revelation 21:24-26 says that the nations will bring their glory into the new Jerusalem. Ruth, a Moabite, was an ancestor of David and Jesus (Matthew 1:5). Acts 17:26-27 says God made all nations that they should seek him.
application:
Pray for a nation that is facing disaster or war.

Consider whether you have grown complacent, like wine left on its dregs, from too much ease.

Do one thing for the Lord with wholehearted effort today and not in slackness.
prayerPrompts: Praise God as God of all nations.
Pray for those who suffer under proud powers.
Ask him not to let you grow complacent.
